newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Britain open talks on new air accord.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain open talks on new air accord.

text.p: U.S. and British officials met throughout the day on Wednesday to see if there was enough common ground to warrant a new bilateral effort to negotiate a "free market" aviation services agreement.
But the officials gave no immediate indication if any progress was made in the opening round of talks.
A second day of talks is planned for Thursday.
Efforts the past two years to remove the many restrictions in the existing bilateral air acccord have ended in failure, most recently in August.
Officials stressed that the two days of talks were preliminary, and only if substantial progress was made would subsequent, more technical talks, be held.
Those would be held in London later this month.
The sticking point on writing a free-market air accord has been winning more landing slots for U.S. carriers at London Heathrow airport.
Ceding slots to American carriers has been fought by the British government, as well as British Airways Plc., U.S. officials say.
The shortage of open slots there has prevented U.S. carriers from increasing their London services.
Now only two U.S. carriers fly into Heathrow, considered a vital transfer point for service beyond to continental Europe, and the rights of U.S. carriers to fly beyond is limited.
The U.S. carriers are American Airlines and United Airlines.
An "open skies" accord is seen vital to a plan by British Airways and American to jointly market their transatlantic services.
The United States has said it would not approve such an alliance -- and the antitrust immunity needed -- without a U.S.-British "open skies" agreement.
